title: Histology of Basic Tissues (ANA 202)
description: Microscopic structure of epithelium, connective tissue, cartilage and bone, muscle and nervous tissue, with basic histological techniques.

topics.title: Epithelial Tissue and Glands
topics.summary: Classification of epithelia, cell junctions, surface specialisations and glands.

notes.b: Epithelia are classified by number of layers (simple or stratified) and shape of surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar). Simple squamous lines alveoli, blood vessels (endothelium) and serous cavities (mesothelium); simple cuboidal lines kidney tubules and thyroid follicles; simple columnar lines the stomach and intestine; pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells lines the trachea and bronchi (respiratory epithelium); stratified squamous keratinised forms the epidermis, non-keratinised lines the oesophagus, mouth and vagina; transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the urinary bladder and ureters. Epithelium rests on a basement membrane and is avascular.

Microvilli (brush border) increase absorptive surface in the small intestine and proximal convoluted tubule; cilia (9+2 microtubules) move mucus; stereocilia are long microvilli in the epididymis. Junctions: tight junctions (zonula occludens) seal; desmosomes (macula adherens) anchor; gap junctions allow communication; hemidesmosomes attach to the basement membrane. Exocrine glands secrete through ducts; endocrine glands secrete into blood. Modes of secretion: merocrine (exocytosis, e.g. salivary glands), apocrine (part of the cell lost, e.g. mammary lipid) and holocrine (whole cell, e.g. sebaceous glands).
k: Tight junctions seal; gap junctions communicate

topics.title: Connective Tissue Proper
topics.summary: Cells, fibres and ground substance of connective tissue and its classification.

notes.b: Connective tissue consists of cells, fibres and ground substance (extracellular matrix). Fixed cells include fibroblasts (make fibres and matrix), adipocytes and macrophages (histiocytes); wandering cells include mast cells (histamine, heparin), plasma cells (antibodies; 'clock-face' chromatin) and leucocytes. Fibres: collagen (type I in skin, bone and tendons; type II in cartilage; type III — reticular fibres — in lymphoid organs and liver; type IV in basement membranes), elastic fibres (elastin and fibrillin; large arteries, lungs) and reticular fibres (argyrophilic, silver-staining). Vitamin C is required for collagen hydroxylation; deficiency causes scurvy.
k: Collagen I: bone/tendon; II: cartilage; III: reticular; IV: basement membrane

notes.b: Loose (areolar) connective tissue fills spaces beneath epithelia. Dense regular connective tissue (parallel collagen) forms tendons and ligaments; dense irregular forms the dermis and organ capsules. Specialised connective tissues include adipose tissue (white — energy store; brown — heat production in newborns, rich in mitochondria), reticular tissue (stroma of lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow), cartilage, bone and blood. Marfan syndrome results from defective fibrillin.

topics.title: Cartilage and Bone
topics.summary: Types of cartilage, bone cells, compact and spongy bone, and ossification.

notes.b: Cartilage is avascular connective tissue with chondrocytes in lacunae, surrounded (except articular and fibrocartilage) by a perichondrium. Hyaline cartilage (type II collagen) is the most common: articular surfaces, costal cartilages, trachea, and the fetal skeleton. Elastic cartilage (with elastic fibres) is in the external ear, epiglottis and auditory tube. Fibrocartilage (type I collagen, no perichondrium) is in intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis and menisci. Cartilage grows by appositional and interstitial growth and heals poorly because it lacks blood vessels.

Bone cells: osteoprogenitor cells, osteoblasts (form osteoid), osteocytes (in lacunae, communicate via canaliculi) and osteoclasts (multinucleated, from the monocyte–macrophage lineage, resorb bone in Howship's lacunae). Compact bone is organised into osteons (Haversian systems) with central Haversian canals connected by Volkmann's canals; spongy (cancellous) bone has trabeculae and houses red marrow. Intramembranous ossification forms flat bones of the skull and the clavicle; endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model (long bones). Growth in length occurs at the epiphyseal plate (zones: resting, proliferation, hypertrophy, calcification, ossification).
k: Intramembranous: skull vault, clavicle; endochondral: long bones

topics.title: Muscle Tissue
topics.summary: Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle: structure, the sarcomere and distinguishing features.

notes.b: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, multinucleated cells with peripheral nuclei and cross-striations. Connective tissue layers: endomysium (around each fibre), perimysium (around fascicles) and epimysium (around the whole muscle). The sarcomere, from Z line to Z line, is the contractile unit: the A band (dark, length of thick myosin filaments) stays constant during contraction, while the I band (thin actin only) and H zone (myosin only) shorten. T-tubules at the A–I junction form triads with the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Satellite cells allow limited regeneration.
k: A band constant; I band and H zone shorten

notes.b: Cardiac muscle cells are striated, branched, with one or two central nuclei, joined end-to-end by intercalated discs containing desmosomes and gap junctions (for synchronous contraction); T-tubules form dyads at the Z line. They cannot regenerate after infarction. Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, non-striated, with a single central nucleus; actin filaments attach to dense bodies. Smooth muscle can divide (hyperplasia), e.g. the uterus in pregnancy.
k: Smooth: spindle-shaped, no striations, dense bodies

topics.title: Nervous Tissue and Histological Techniques
topics.summary: Neurons, neuroglia and myelination, plus tissue preparation and staining.

notes.b: Neurons have a cell body (perikaryon) containing Nissl bodies (rough ER), dendrites and a single axon arising from the axon hillock (which lacks Nissl substance). Types: multipolar (motor neurons), bipolar (retina, olfactory epithelium), pseudounipolar (dorsal root ganglia). Neuroglia: astrocytes (blood–brain barrier support), oligodendrocytes (myelinate several CNS axons), microglia (CNS macrophages, mesodermal origin), ependymal cells (line ventricles), and in the PNS Schwann cells (each myelinates one internode of one axon) and satellite cells. Nodes of Ranvier allow saltatory conduction.
k: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin; Schwann cells: PNS myelin

notes.b: Routine tissue processing: fixation (10% neutral buffered formalin, which cross-links proteins), dehydration in ascending alcohols, clearing (xylene), infiltration and embedding in paraffin wax, sectioning with a microtome (about 3–5 µm), and staining. Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is the routine stain: haematoxylin (basic) stains acidic structures such as nuclei blue/purple (basophilic); eosin (acidic) stains cytoplasm and collagen pink (eosinophilic). Special stains: PAS for glycogen and mucin (magenta), Masson's trichrome for collagen, silver for reticular fibres, Sudan black/oil red O for fat (on frozen sections).
k: Order: fix → dehydrate → clear → embed → section → stain
PAS: glycogen; oil red O: fat
